lead: Ephesians describes Easter happening in us: we were dead through our trespasses, and God, “rich in mercy”, made us alive together with Christ, raised us up with him and seated us with him. In the Gospel Jesus rebukes a fever, and Simon's mother-in-law gets up at once and serves. Both readings have the same movement: lying down, raised up, and then service. We are saved by grace, and grace sets us to work.

r.h: By grace you have been saved
set: Ephesians is a letter of praise and teaching that bears Paul's name, addressed to Christians of Gentile background. Many scholars think it comes from a disciple who gathered Paul's thought after his death; many others hold that Paul wrote it from prison (3:1; 4:1). Chapter 1 has just praised the power God showed when he raised Christ from the dead and seated him at his right hand (1:20). Chapter 2 says that the same power has been at work in the readers.
str: vv. 1–3: what we were: dead, following the course of this world, children of wrath.
vv. 4–7: but God: made alive with Christ, raised with him, seated with him.
vv. 8–9: saved by grace, through faith, as a gift, not as the result of works.
v. 10: God's handiwork, created for good works.
kw: One of three verbs that Ephesians forms with “together with” (syn-): made alive with, raised with, seated with (vv. 5–6). What happened to Christ at Easter is shared with those who belong to him.
God's favour, given without our deserving it. The word appears three times in this short passage (vv. 5, 7, 8).
From the verb “to make”; our word “poem” comes from it. Christians are God's handiwork, his work of art, made new in Christ.
vv: But God, who is rich in mercy, out of the great love with which he loved us
The turning point of the passage is two words: “But God”. Everything before them is human failure; everything after them is God's initiative.
For by grace you have been saved through faith, and this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God
Grace is the source, and faith is the way we receive it. The whole gift, faith included, comes from God.
For we are what he has made us, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand to be our way of life.
Works do not earn salvation, but they are its purpose. God prepared them beforehand, and by his grace we walk in them, so that the good we do is both his gift and truly ours.
ch: The Catechism teaches that our justification comes from the grace of God, the undeserved help he gives us to respond to his call (CCC 1996), and that our merit before God comes from his having chosen to associate us with the work of his grace, so that the merit of good works is to be credited first to the grace of God (CCC 2008). The Council of Trent taught that nothing that comes before justification, whether faith or works, merits the grace of justification (Session 6, chapter 8). In 1999 the Catholic Church and the Lutheran World Federation affirmed together, in their Joint Declaration, that by grace alone, in faith in Christ's saving work and not because of any merit of ours, we are accepted by God.

set: Jesus has just taught in the synagogue at Capernaum on the sabbath and delivered a man from an unclean spirit (4:31–37). Now he goes to Simon's house. Luke has not yet told the call of Simon (5:1–11), so this healing in his home comes before Simon leaves his nets. Simon was married: Paul mentions that Cephas was accompanied by a believing wife (1 Corinthians 9:5).
The sabbath ended at sunset. Only then could people carry their sick through the streets, and so the whole town comes “as the sun was setting”.
str: vv. 38–39: in Simon's house: the fever rebuked, the woman raised, her service.
v. 40: at sunset: the sick brought, hands laid on each one.
v. 41: demons driven out and silenced.
kw: Luke uses the same verb for the demon in 4:35 and for the demons in 4:41. The fever is treated like a hostile power, and Jesus speaks to it with authority.
The verb from which “deacon” comes. Her healing is complete: she takes up her place in the household and serves Jesus and the others. The tense suggests service that goes on.
Only Luke notes that Jesus laid his hands on “each of them” (v. 40). No one is healed as a face in a crowd.
vv: Then he stood over her and rebuked the fever, and it left her.
Mark says that Jesus took her by the hand and lifted her up (Mark 1:31). Luke shows the Lord standing over the sick bed and speaking a word of command.
Immediately she got up and began to serve them.
The Greek for “got up” (anastasa) is from the same family as the word for resurrection. Read in Easter week, she is a picture of every Christian: raised up in order to serve.
and he laid his hands on each of them and cured them.
A long evening, one person at a time.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Christ the physician, moved by so much suffering, not only lets himself be touched by the sick but makes their miseries his own, and that he often uses signs such as the laying on of hands (CCC 1503–1504). The Church continues this care in the Anointing of the Sick, which St James describes (James 5:14–15; CCC 1510).

study: Ephesians says that God prepared good works beforehand for me to walk in. What good work is waiting for me this week?
Simon's mother-in-law got up and served at once. When God has lifted me out of an illness or a trouble, how have I used that new strength?
